# Delegating a key scoped to one template tag

A grant may name a scope. A key whose actions are scoped to one template tag can
run that resource's whole lifecycle and is refused on every other resource,
including when the request names it by content hash rather than by tag.

## Mint the scoped key

```bash
rimsky auth init --endpoint "$BASE"
```

`tenant-alpha.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "tenant-alpha",
  "description": "Least-privilege delegation: the full template lifecycle, but only for the alpha tag.",
  "permissions": [
    {"action": "*:read"},
    {"action": "template:register",   "scope": {"template_tag": "alpha"}},
    {"action": "template:deploy",     "scope": {"template_tag": "alpha"}},
    {"action": "template:undeploy",   "scope": {"template_tag": "alpha"}},
    {"action": "template:deregister", "scope": {"template_tag": "alpha"}},
    {"action": "tag:set",             "scope": {"template_tag": "alpha"}},
    {"action": "tag:delete",          "scope": {"template_tag": "alpha"}},
    {"action": "instance:create",     "scope": {"template_tag": "alpha"}}
  ]
}
```

```bash
rimsky auth create-key --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN" \
  --name tenant-alpha --role-file tenant-alpha.json

rimsky auth show tenant-alpha --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN"
```

All seven scoped entries read back carrying the `alpha` scope.

## Drive the whole lifecycle, in scope and out

Every call below is made with the tenant key. The `beta` tag belongs to the
admin.

```bash
tenant() { curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TENANT" -H 'content-type: application/json' "$@"; }
```

| Action | In scope (`alpha`) | Out of scope (`beta`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/templates` | 201 | 403 |
| `POST /v1/templates/{id}/deploy` | 200 | 403 |
| `PUT /v1/tags/{tag}` | 200 | 403 |
| `DELETE /v1/tags/{tag}` | 200 | 403 |
| `POST /v1/instances` by tag | created | 403 |
| `POST /v1/instances` by template hash | created | 403 |
| `POST /v1/templates/{id}/undeploy` | 200 | 403 |
| `DELETE /v1/templates/{id}` | 200 | 403 |

Naming the resource by its content hash does not evade the scope: the hash
resolves through the tag rows, so the out-of-scope hash is refused too.

The beta template survives every out-of-scope attempt and still reads 200 for
the admin.

## The key stays a working key

```bash
tenant -X GET "$BASE/v1/templates"                                  # 200
tenant -X POST "$BASE/v1/auth/keys" -d '{"name":"probe","permissions":[{"action":"*"}]}'  # 403
```

The unscoped `*:read` grant keeps working while the scoped actions are refused
outside their scope. The delegation is narrow, not broken.
